H1.text: A rubber ball bounces back high. A cricket ball bounces less. A lump of dough just goes splat.

H2.text: Same floor, same drop. Very different bounces.

H3.text: Diya drops three balls from one metre onto the kitchen floor. A rubber ball, a cloth ball, and a lump of dough.

H4.text: The rubber ball comes back to eighty one centimetres. The cloth ball, to thirty six. The dough, to zero. Can one number describe each bounce?

H5.text: It can. It is called the coefficient of restitution.

P1.text: Restitution means giving back. How much speed does a collision give back?

P2.text: We compare two speeds. The speed of separation: how fast the bodies move apart after the hit. And the speed of approach: how fast they came together.

P3.text: e equals the speed of separation divided by the speed of approach. Both are speeds, so e has no unit.

S1.text: Our motion notebook. The rubber ball falls from one metre. g is nine point eight.

S2.text: It hits the floor at four point four three metres per second.

S3.text: It leaves at three point nine eight. The floor does not move, so e is three point nine eight over four point four three. Zero point nine.

S4.text: It rises to eighty one centimetres. Every new bounce is lower, by the same factor each time.

S5.text: Slow-mo replay. Freeze at the floor.

S6.text: Coming in, four point four three, downward. Going out, three point nine eight, upward.

S7.text: The ball squashes and springs back, but not all the way. A little energy stays behind as heat and sound.

S8.text: Now the cloth ball. e is zero point six. It rises to only thirty six centimetres.

S9.text: And the dough. e is zero. It hits, and stays. Nothing is given back.

D1.text: Why do the heights follow e squared? Step by step.

D2.text: Step one. Falling from height h, the ball hits the floor at v equals root two g h.

D3.text: Step two. It bounces off at e times v.

D4.text: Step three. It rises to height h one, where e v equals root two g h one.

D5.text: Step four. Divide the two. e equals root of h one over h. So h one equals e squared times h.

D6.text: For the rubber ball, zero point nine squared is zero point eight one. Eighty one centimetres.

T1.text: Remember this. e is the speed apart, divided by the speed of approach. It lies between zero and one.

R1.text: Now, how does e connect the collisions we know? Link by link.

R2.text: e equals one: they part as fast as they met. Kinetic energy is kept. That is an elastic collision.

R3.text: e equals zero: they do not part at all. They stick. That is perfectly inelastic.

R4.text: Between zero and one: some bounce, some energy lost. Almost every real collision lives here.

K1.text: Side by side. On the left, a ball hits a still wall at ten metres per second, and comes back at five. e is five over ten, one half.

K2.text: On the right, cart A at six chases cart B at two. They close in at four. After the hit, A has three and B has five. They part at two. e is two over four, one half again.

K3.text: Now you try. A ball hits the floor, and rises to one quarter of the height it fell from. Is e one quarter, or one half? Pause and decide.

K4.text: One half! Height goes as e squared. One half squared is one quarter.

W2.text: A two kilogram ball at six metres per second hits a still one kilogram ball, head on. e is zero point five. Find both velocities.

W3.text: Momentum: twelve equals two v one, plus v two.

W4.text: Restitution: v two minus v one equals zero point five times six. That is three.

W5.text: Put v two equals v one plus three into the first line. Three v one plus three equals twelve. So v one is three, and v two is six.

W6.text: Check the energy. Thirty six joules before, nine plus eighteen after. Nine joules lost, because e is less than one.

X2.text: Many students take e as one ball's speed after, divided by its speed before.

X3.text: That works only when the other body stays still, like a floor. In general, use the speed apart over the speed of approach.

E1.text: Where is this asked? In bouncing ball numericals, heights after many bounces, and two equation collision problems.

Q1.text: Exam level now. A ball is dropped from five metres. e is zero point five. What total distance does it travel before it comes to rest? Pause and solve.

A1.text: The answer is B. Eight point three three metres.

A2.text: The first fall is five metres. After that, each bounce goes up and down, and each rise is a quarter of the one before.

A3.text: The rises add up: one point two five, plus a quarter of that, and so on. That is five thirds of a metre.

A4.text: Up and down doubles it, to three point three three. Add the first five. Eight point three three metres.
